Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. 1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)

goal.objective:
`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.
